items.title: #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
items.summary: Advisory at a Glance Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware Original Publication October 20, 2026 Executive Summary This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Following, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks. Affected Products CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Key Actions Regularly patch and update systems, especially firewalls, and other edge devices. Implement Zero Trust Principle. Restrict administrative tools and privileges to necessary users only. Strengthen account security by implementing identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies and multifactor authentication (MFA). Indicators of Compromise For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: AA26-293A STIX XML (40 KB) AA26-293A STIX JSON (38 KB) Intended Audience Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts , vulnerability analysts , security systems managers , and operational technology (OT) owners and operators Introduction Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026. Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors. The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents. Download the PDF version of this report: #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware (PDF, 1.02 MB ) For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: AA26-293A-STIX XML (XML, 40.23 KB ) AA26-293A-STIX JSON (JSON, 37.49 KB ) Technical Details Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK ® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques. Initial Access The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [ TA0001 ] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [ T1110 ], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products: CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [ T1190 ] for initial access through automated scripts: CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [ T1098 ], or on newly created accounts [ T1136 ], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [ T1218 ], such as PsExec [ T1021.002 ] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [ T1021.006 ], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1 —a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [ T1059.001 , T1059.003 ]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe , a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares. As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [ T1685 ] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [ T1027.002 ]. Privilege Escalation The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [ T1548.002 ] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [ T1059 ]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [ T1134.001 ]. Lateral Movement To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [ TA0010 ] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [ T1569.002 ] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [ T1021.001 , T1133 ] to expand their presence within the compromised network [ T1021 ]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed. Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [ T1560.001 ], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [ T1048 ] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [ T1567 ]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [ T1490 ]. Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [ T1486 ] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay ) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [ T1070.004 ]. Leveraged Tools Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations. Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control. Table 1. Tools Leveraged by SafePay Threat Actors Tool Name Description 7-Zip An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement. FileZilla An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration. Mimikatz A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [ T1550.002 ]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration. PowerShell A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. PsExec A tool designed to run programs that SafePay threat actors use to execute commands on remote systems. RClone A legitimate command-line program used to sync files with cloud storage services, such as Mega. SafePay threat actors maliciously use RClone for data packaging and movement. ScreenConnect A remote support, access, and meeting software that allows users to control devices remotely over the internet. SafePay threat actors use ScreenConnect for persistence and access. ShareFinder.ps1 A PowerShell script used to scan an Active Directory network for shared folders. SafePay threat actors use ShareFinder.ps1 for exfiltration hunting. WinRAR Archive utility used to split compromised data into segments and to compress [ T1560.001 ] files into a .RAR format prior to exfiltration. SafePay threat actors use WinRAR for data packaging and movement. WinRM A Windows-based protocol designed to facilitate remote management and automation. SafePay threat actors use WinRM for command execution. AnyDesk and TeamViewer Legitimate remote desktop tool used for accessing and controlling computers over the internet. SafePay threat actors use AnyDesk and TeamViewer to transfer malware to the victim’s system. AcronisDiskDirector A legitimate disk management tool. SharpShares.exe A network scanning tool used for host discovery and enumeration. NetExec A legitimate network assessment tool to enumerate systems, validate credentials, and manage remote operations across private networks. Backblaze A command-line tool for file management within Backblaze B2 cloud storage. SafePay threat actors executed commands via b2.exe to exfiltrate a victim’s data. Indicators of Compromise Table 2 through Table 5 list IOCs associated with SafePay ransomware that allowed for the identification of malicious activity. Disclaimer: The authoring agencies recommend organizations investigate or verify IP addresses prior to taking action, such as blocking. These IOCs were observed between November 2024 and August 2026. The authoring organizations recommend organizations investigate or verify tool use prior to taking action, such as blocking. Table 3. Malicious Files Filename Description 1 - Copy.bat A batch script likely used to copy, stage, or move files during lateral movement or data collection. DYRasWtb.exe A suspected malicious executable. libsmb2.dll A library associated with Server Message Block (SMB) communication; may support lateral movement or file transfer. In some cases, SafePay threat actors deleted all network-attached backups of company data. Incident Response If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions: Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion . Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc. Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force ) (see the Reporting section for contact information). Apply eviction countermeasures , including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network ( Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet. Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance). If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide . Mitigations The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections. Organizations should implement the following mitigations: Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date , as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [ CPG 2.B ]. Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases. Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [ CPG 3.F ]. Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines ; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [ CPG 3.B ]. Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length. Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers. Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials. Avoid reusing passwords [ CPG 3.C ]. Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [ CPG 3.E ]. Disable password “hints.” Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year. Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher. Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [ CPG 3.O ]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable. Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [ CPG 3.K ]. Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [ CPG 3.I , 3.O , 1.C ]. Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [ CPG 3.I ]. Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [ CPG 4.B ]. To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host. Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence. Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts. Disable unused ports . Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization. Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [ CPG 3.G ]. Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher ; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model ). This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need. Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task. Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [ CPG 3.M ]. These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software . CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates. Validate Security Controls In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory. To get started: Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16 ). Align your security technologies against the technique. Test your technologies against the technique. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process. The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory. Resources Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts. CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices. CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA. CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack. USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident. CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks. CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection. Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices. CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance CISA’s CI Fortify: Strengthening Resilience Across Critical Infrastructure CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre U.K.’s National Crime Agency Reporting Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws. The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file. Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators. The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) , a local FBI field office , a local USSS Field Office , or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center ( contact@cisa.dhs.gov ) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force , or use the non-emergency number 101. Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. CISA and the FBI/USSS do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favoring by the FBI, CISA, or USSS. The authoring agencies recognize that infrastructure used for malicious activity may be hosted on cloud or virtualized platforms where IP addresses can be dynamically or temporarily assigned. As a result, an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services. Accordingly, these indicators should be interpreted as historically observed infrastructure within the activity window and should be corroborated with current network telemetry or additional intelligence sources when used for defensive or investigative purposes. General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. items.title: Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product
items.summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect MicroSCADA X SYS600 product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to carry out various attacks on the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product are affected: MicroSCADA X SYS600 vers:MicroSCADA_X_SYS600/<=10.7, 10.8 (CVE-2026-9852, CVE-2026-9853, CVE-2026-9854, CVE-2026-9853) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File, Incorrect Implementation of Authentication Algorithm Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-9852 A CSV injection vulnerability exists in SYS600. Injected malicious formulas can add or modify data to the spreadsheet, insert links, exfiltrate data, and in some cases, depending on how the user has their environment configured, execute malicious code on the user’s machine. To exploit this issue attackers would need a way to create arbitrary log messages. This could be achieved through normal functionality via SCIL scripts, a log injection vulnerability, or via the SYS600 broker. This vulnerability affects all Windows users regardless of their privilege level who can run the Notify service and export the log. items.title: HMS Networks PEAK-System PCAN Windows drivers
items.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could crash the Windows kernel. The following versions of HMS Networks PEAK-System PCAN Windows drivers are affected: PEAK-System Device Driver Setup <=5.1.2.1151 (CVE-2026-109576, CVE-2026-101103, CVE-2026-94188, CVE-2026-103672, CVE-2026-110322, CVE-2026-105960) PCAN Windows CAN device drivers <=5.1.2 (CVE-2026-109576, CVE-2026-101103, CVE-2026-94188, CVE-2026-103672, CVE-2026-110322, CVE-2026-105960) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.1 HMS Networks PEAK-System Device Driver Setup 5 Vulnerabilities Out-of-bounds Write, Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow'), Improper Validation of Array Index, Untrusted Pointer Dereference, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Transportation Systems, Healthcare and Public Health, Energy, Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Sweden Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-109576 The parser in PEAK-System PCAN driver correctly detected the malformed record, but the loop iterating the record list advanced its processed-bytes counter even when a record had been rejected as invalid. items.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation
items.summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), National Security Agency’s Super Intelligence Security Center (NSA SISC) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation . The product outlines ten voluntary core practices to help organizations that train and evaluate highly capable super intelligence (SI) agents—particularly pre-deployment, cutting edge SI agents with reduced safeguards or other high-risk, non-public systems—prepare for and manage SI control incidents. A SI control incident occurs when one or more SI agents takes uninstructed actions that conflict with or compromise policies, controls, or security measures that scope the task and provide human oversight. This product aligns with cyber incident response best practices, includes additional SI considerations and highlights the importance of testing controls and validating containment before resuming SI agent activities. It addresses: measures for limiting agent access to information, systems, tools, and networks; monitoring for unexpected activity; preserving evidence and shutting down undesired behavior; rebuilding from verified baselines; and reporting incidents and near-misses to relevant government agencies and affected parties. For more information and resources visit CISA’s Super Intelligence page.

items.title: Cyber Threat Actors Use a Variety of Techniques to Target Election and Campaign Officials
items.summary: CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a Public Service Announcement (PSA) warning election and campaign officials about cyber threats during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Malicious cyber actors may use phishing and smishing techniques to steal login credentials and other sensitive information or install malware on targeted devices. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations may be attractive targets because of their access to voter registration data, current government officials, and sensitive campaign information. Cyber actors are increasingly using sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications. These efforts may include convincing emails, text messages, audio, and video content designed to manipulate recipients into disclosing sensitive information or interacting with malicious links and attachments. CISA and the FBI urge election officials, campaign personnel, and the public to review the PSA, follow recommended cybersecurity practices, and remain vigilant for suspicious emails and mobile messages.

items.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-61624 Fortinet Multiple Products Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: CISA Urges Patching Critical Vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support
items.summary: CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 , affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05 . Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. Organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances should conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends taking the following actions: Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances. Collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or forensic image for physical appliances to conduct future forensics, immediately forward appliance syslog and session events to the SIEM, and collect any additional logs, such as web application firewall, reverse-proxy, or perimeter firewall logs for the exposure window. Consult BeyondTrust’s Syslog guide for additional information on forwarding appliance logs and session events. Conduct network and forensic investigations for evidence of compromise. Additionally, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, unrecognized script files, unexpected gaps in logs or log forwarding, and unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes. Consult CISA’s Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to assist with prioritizing vulnerability remediation. Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. Then rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new multifactor authentication registrations on privileged accounts. CISA urges organizations to review the BeyondTrust security advisory and resources noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing Mandiant’s blog, ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust , for additional hunt and isolation guidance and detections. items.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-21589 Atlassian Multiple Products Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: CISA Malcolm
items.summary: View CSAF Summary The following versions of CISA Malcolm are affected: Malcolm <=v26.07.1 (CVE-2026-107336, CVE-2026-107361, CVE-2026-107337, CVE-2026-107335, CVE-2026-107334) Malcolm <=v26.08.0 (CVE-2026-107333, CVE-2026-107362) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 CISA Malcolm 6 Vulnerabilities Authentication Bypass by Spoofing, Incorrect Authorization, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy, Information Technology, Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-107336 Malcolm's front nginx reverse proxy defines a "Dashboards → Arkime shortcut" location using a case-insensitive regex matcher but a case-sensitive rewrite. A request whose path segment is not exact-lowercase (for example /IDDASH2ARK/...) enters the location (the matcher fires) but evades the rewrite (no redirect is issued), so nginx falls through to the location's proxy_pass to the Arkime backend. That location is the one proxied location in the shipped config that does not include the per-location authentication file, so the request reaches Arkime unauthenticated. The same location also forwards a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User header un-overwritten, and Arkime is configured to trust X-Forwarded-User as the authenticated username — so an unauthenticated network caller can reach the Arkime backend while supplying a forged, auto-provisioned identity. An authenticated user can craft a specially formatted request path to bypass role-based restrictions and reach administrative or role gated endpoints they should not have access to. This affects all restricted paths protected by the RBAC authorization layer, including file upload, PHP server, htadmin, and authentication management interfaces. items.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-0322 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 Cisco Secure Email Gateway Relative Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-105133 Ahsay AhsayCBS Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-105134 Ahsay AhsayCBS Command Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: CISA Urges Patching Newly Exploited Vulnerability in Ivanti Connect Secure
items.summary: CISA is aware of Ivanti’s disclosure of a newly exploited vulnerability, CVE-2026-104935 , affecting Ivanti Connect Secure versions 25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, and 22.8R2.4 and prior. CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration. CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Oct. 13, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and deployments to immediately update to the latest version, as outlined in Ivanti’s Security Advisory Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2026-104935) . Organizations should also review the Ivanti Connect Secure 25.x Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for detailed patching guidance for hardware and virtual appliance deployments. Ivanti Connect Secure version 22.8 reaches end of life on Jan. 31, 2027. Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation. Note: Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect evidence of exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 because threat actor commands execute in memory. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends implementing the following actions from Ivanti Connect Secure Recovery Procedures : Create a backup of the appliance configuration. Review Ivanti’s How to Backup & Restore the Binary Configuration Using Archiving Server for more information. Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. CISA urges organizations to review the Ivanti security advisory and guide noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing the Volexity blog, A Series of Unauthenticated Events: Chained Exploitation of Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days . Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. items.title: Red Lion Controls N-Tron 700 Series (Update A)
items.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow a malicious user to access the device and gain administrative access. This access would allow the user to view, edit, and upload configuration files. Further, a malicious user can cause the switch to reboot by navigating to a specific URL on the device. This action can be scripted on the malicious user's local machine to cause continuous rebooting of the switch. The following versions of Red Lion Controls N-Tron 700 Series are affected: 700 Series <=Firmware_3.11.0 (CVE-2026-32645, CVE-2026-39460, CVE-2026-28745, CVE-2026-33367, CVE-2026-29797, CVE-2026-39453, CVE-2026-33272) 700 Series <=Bootloader_2.0.6.1 (CVE-2026-32645, CVE-2026-39460, CVE-2026-28745, CVE-2026-33367, CVE-2026-29797, CVE-2026-39453, CVE-2026-33272) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.3 Red Lion Controls 700 Series 7 Vulnerabilities Use of Hard-coded Credentials, Insufficiently Protected Credentials, Storing Passwords in a Recoverable Format, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Download of Code Without Integrity Check, Reachable Assertion, Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities, Communications, Critical Manufacturing, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Sweden Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-32645 Default factory credentials with administrative access are enabled and persist even after configuring other administrator accounts. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.
